newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden seeks low nickel content in euro coins.
newsitem.headline: Sweden seeks low nickel content in euro coins.

text.p: Sweden reiterated a call on Monday for having as little nickel as possible in future euro coins, arguing the metal could cause health problems.
The issue was debated during a meeting of European Union finance ministers. Finance Minister Erik Asbrink did not rule out a decision on the sensitive issue later in the day.
Euro coins are due to enter circulation in 2002 in countries participating in the European Union's economic and monetary union (EMU).
Sweden seeks to reduce the nickel content as far as possible in the planned coins because of health reasons, saying it can cause allergic reactions.
Asbrink said Sweden could not accept a decision which meant that there would be a lot of nickel in the new coins.
"This is an important question for Sweden," he said, adding he believed several countries would show an understanding for Stockholm's position.
But, he added, "there is no doubt that there is a varying degree of awareness about the health problems...I am convinced that time is on our side."
Asbrink also said Sweden had shown that there was a good alternative in the country's 10-crown coin which instead of nickel included a metal mix called "Nordic gold", consisting mainly of copper.
However, other countries want to make the content of the euro coins the same as for most existing world currencies in order to facilitate recycling.
